decks.title: Theory of Supply — Part 1: Supply, its Determinants and the Law of Supply
goals: Distinguish stock from supply for perishable and durable goods
Write the supply function and explain the determinants of supply
State the law of supply, derive market supply and explain its exceptions

slides.heading: Theory of Supply and Elasticity of Supply
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what **supply** means, how it differs from **stock**, what **determines** it, and the **law of supply**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: supply and stock, determinants, the supply function, the law of supply, market supply and its exceptions
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Demand tells us what buyers want. Supply is the other half of every market. A weaver in Surat, a fisherman in Kochi and a cement plant in Satna all decide how much to offer for sale. In this part we see what supply means, how it differs from the stock a seller holds, what affects it, and the law that links it to price.

slides.heading: What supply means
slides.body_md:
**Supply** is the quantity of a good that sellers are **willing and able to offer for sale** at a given **price** during a given **period**.

It is a **flow**: a quantity per day, week or month at a stated price.

visual.alt: Flow: supply needs a price and a period, which together give the quantity offered for sale
visual.caption: Supply needs a price and a period

slides.narration: Supply is not the same as production or the goods lying in a godown. It is the amount sellers actually offer for sale, at a particular price, during a particular period. A statement like a weaver supplies fifty sarees means nothing until we add at what price and in how much time.

slides.heading: Stock and supply
columns:
**Stock** is the **total quantity** a seller **holds** at a point of time.

**Supply** is the part of the stock **offered for sale** at a price.
For **perishables** (fish, flowers), supply is close to stock. For **durables** (furniture, steel), sellers can **hold back** stock when they expect better prices.

rows: Perishable: must sell almost all today
Durable: holds back 180 for a better price

visual.alt: Table comparing stock and supply: an imagined Kochi fisherman has a stock of 500 kilograms and supplies all of it because fish is perishable; an imagined Saharanpur dealer has 300 boxes but supplies 120, holding back 180 because boxes are durable
visual.caption: Supply can equal stock but never exceed it in the short period.

slides.narration: Stock is everything the seller has. Supply is what he puts on sale at today's price. A fisherman without an ice box must sell nearly all his catch today, so his supply is almost his whole stock. A woodcraft dealer can wait, so he offers only part of his stock and keeps the rest for a better price.

slides.heading: Quick check: a perishable catch
slides.body_md: A Kochi fisherman with no ice box must sell before evening. His supply is most likely…
slides.narration: Can he keep the fish for next week? If not, how much of his stock will he offer today?

slides.heading: Determinants of supply
slides.body_md: Besides its **own price**, supply depends on **input prices**, **technology**, **taxes and subsidies**, the **goal of the firm**, **prices of related goods** and the **number of firms**.

visual.alt: Table of the determinants of supply: own price, prices of inputs, technology, taxes and subsidies, the goal of the firm, prices of related goods and the number of firms, with the direction of their effect on supply

slides.narration: Many things decide how much a firm offers. Its own price matters most. But cheaper inputs, better technology or a subsidy let it offer more at every price, while a tax or dearer inputs make it offer less. A firm chasing market share offers more than one chasing only profit, and more firms mean more market supply.

slides.heading: The supply function
slides.body_md: **Sx = f(Px, Pf, T, Tx, G, Pr, N)**

nodes.label: Input prices Pf, technology T, taxes Tx
Goal G, related goods Pr, firms N

visual.alt: Flow showing the supply function: the own price, input prices, technology, taxes, the goal of the firm, prices of related goods and the number of firms all feed into the quantity supplied
visual.caption: Sx = f(Px, Pf, T, Tx, G, Pr, N)

slides.narration: We can write all of this as a supply function. The quantity of X supplied depends on its own price, the prices of factors, technology, taxes, the goal of the firm, prices of related goods and the number of firms. When we draw a supply curve, we let only the own price change and hold the rest constant.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a dairy's choices
slides.body_md: A dairy cooperative in an imagined Anand village can make paneer or ghee. Predict its supply of paneer when (i) ghee becomes dearer, (ii) fodder becomes cheaper.
bullets: Step 1 — Is the change in paneer's own price? No, so the curve shifts.
Step 2 — Ghee competes for the same milk: paneer supply decreases.
Step 3 — Cheaper fodder lowers cost: paneer supply increases.

visual.alt: Worked example table for an imagined Anand dairy: a rise in the ghee price decreases paneer supply because ghee competes for the same milk, while cheaper fodder increases paneer supply because it lowers cost

slides.narration: Ask first whether the paneer price itself has changed. It has not, so the whole supply curve will move. Ghee uses the same milk, so when ghee pays better, milk moves to ghee and paneer supply falls. Cheaper fodder lowers the cost of milk, so the dairy can offer more paneer at every price.

slides.heading: The law of supply
slides.body_md:
Other things remaining the same, the **quantity supplied rises when the price rises** and **falls when the price falls**.

The supply curve therefore **slopes upward** from left to right.

slides.narration: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, other things constant. A higher price makes extra output worth producing, even though the extra units cost more to make. So the supply curve slopes upward. Here the weaver offers forty sarees at five hundred rupees and fifty-two at six hundred.

slides.heading: Quick check: more bakeries
slides.body_md: Twelve new bakeries open in a Mysuru town. Market supply of bread will…
slides.narration: Market supply adds up all sellers. What happens to the total when there are more sellers?

slides.heading: Market supply: add across
slides.body_md: At each price, **add the quantities** of all firms: the **horizontal sum**.

visual.alt: Supply schedules of three imagined Ludhiana knitting units and their market supply: at 100, 200, 300 and 400 rupees a packet the market supplies 15, 45, 75, 105 packets, the sums of the units' quantities at each price
visual.caption: Imagined figures: market supply = sum of quantities at each price.

slides.narration: The market supply schedule adds the quantities of all firms at the same price. At three hundred rupees a packet the three knitting units offer thirty, twenty-five and twenty packets, so the market offers seventy-five. Notice that one unit offers nothing at the lowest price, because that price does not cover its cost.

Step 3 — Join the totals: the market curve lies to the right.

slides.narration: The law of supply has exceptions. Labour is one. As the wage rises, a worker first offers more hours. But beyond a high wage, she may prefer more leisure to more income, so she works fewer hours. Her supply curve of labour bends backward. Here, above four hundred rupees an hour, the translator works less.

slides.heading: Other exceptions to the law of supply

rows: A Chennai surgeon cuts her hours after a fee rise
A Guntur chilli trader withholds stock
Sells less now to sell later at more

visual.alt: Table of four exceptions to the law of supply: labour at high wages, rare goods, agricultural goods in the short period and an expected future price rise, each with an imagined example and the reason

slides.narration: Rare goods such as old coins cannot be increased, however high the price. A farmer cannot raise this season's crop once it is sown. And a trader who expects prices to rise next month may sell less now, even if the current price has gone up. In each case quantity supplied does not rise with price.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Quantity offered at a price in a period; at most the stock
Own price, input prices, technology, taxes, goals, related goods, firms
Price and quantity supplied move together; curve slopes up
Horizontal sum of firms' supplies; exceptions exist

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of supply and stock, the determinants, the law of supply and market supply with exceptions

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Supply is the quantity offered for sale at a price in a period, and it can never exceed the stock. It depends on the own price and on many other factors. The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move together. Market supply is the horizontal sum of firms' supplies, and there are some exceptions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define supply with **price** and **period**; contrast it with **stock** using a perishable and a durable example.
Write the supply function in symbols before explaining determinants.
For each determinant, state the **direction** (increase or decrease) and the **reason** (cost or reward).
Market supply: **add quantities at each price**; never add prices.
Exceptions: give the reason why quantity does not rise with price.
slides.narration: Examiners look for a few things. Always mention price and period when you define supply. Write the supply function in symbols. For each determinant, say which way supply moves and why, usually through cost. When you build market supply, add quantities at each price. For exceptions, explain the reason, not just the name.

goals: Distinguish extension and contraction from increase and decrease of supply
Calculate elasticity of supply by the percentage method
Identify the degree of elasticity of a straight supply line by the geometric method

slides.heading: Theory of Supply, Part 2
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **movement along** versus **shift** of the supply curve, and **elasticity of supply**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: movement along the curve, shift of the curve, elasticity of supply, the percentage method and the geometric method
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 2 we separate two kinds of change in supply: moving along a supply curve and moving the whole curve. Then we ask how strongly sellers respond to price, which is the elasticity of supply, and learn to measure it by the percentage method and to read it from a diagram.

slides.heading: Movement along versus shift
columns:
**Movement along the curve:** only the **own price** changes.

- Higher price → **extension**
- Lower price → **contraction**

**Shift of the curve:** another **determinant** changes.

- More at every price → **increase**
- Less at every price → **decrease**

rows: Change in the good's own price
Extension: more at a higher price
Contraction: less at a lower price

visual.alt: Table distinguishing a movement along the supply curve (extension and contraction, caused by the own price) from a shift of the curve (increase and decrease, caused by other determinants)

slides.narration: Two changes are easily confused. If only the good's own price changes, the seller moves along the same curve: up is an extension, down is a contraction. If anything else changes, such as costs, taxes or technology, the whole curve moves: to the right is an increase, to the left a decrease.

Does it lower cost or raise the reward of supplying?

slides.narration: To decide the direction of a shift, ask one question. Does the change make supplying cheaper or more rewarding? Cheaper inputs, better technology, a subsidy or more firms shift supply right. Dearer inputs, a tax, a more attractive competing product or fewer firms shift it left.

slides.heading: Elasticity of supply
slides.body_md:
**Elasticity of supply (Es)** is the degree of responsiveness of **quantity supplied** to a change in the good's **own price**.

Es = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price.

nodes.label: Divide the first by the second

visual.alt: Flow of the percentage method for elasticity of supply: divide the change in quantity supplied by the original quantity, divide the change in price by the original price, divide the first by the second and compare with one
visual.caption: Es = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P)

slides.narration: Elasticity of supply measures how strongly sellers respond to a change in price. We compare the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in price. Because both usually move in the same direction, the coefficient is normally positive. A large value means sellers respond strongly.

slides.narration: Three cases are special. A horizontal supply line is perfectly elastic: at the given price any quantity is offered. slides.narration: Between the extremes lie two more degrees. If quantity responds more than in proportion to price, supply is relatively elastic. sections.heading: 1. Supply and stock
sections.body_md:
**Supply** is the quantity a seller is willing and able to **offer for sale** at a given **price** in a given **period**. **Stock** is the total quantity held at a point of time.

- Supply can at most **equal** stock in the short period.
- **Perishable** goods: supply is close to stock.
- **Durable** goods: sellers may **hold back** stock and supply less.

key_terms.definition_md: Quantity offered for sale at a given price during a given period.
Total quantity of a good held by a seller at a point of time.

rows: Perishable: must sell almost all today
Durable: holds back 180 for a better price

sections.heading: 2. Determinants of supply and the supply function
sections.body_md:
**Sx = f(Px, Pf, T, Tx, G, Pr, N)**: own price, prices of factors, technology, taxes and subsidies, goal of the firm, prices of related goods, number of firms.

Lower costs (cheaper inputs, better technology, subsidies), a sales goal and more firms **increase** supply; higher costs, taxes and dearer competing products **decrease** it.

Another product that uses the same resources, such as wheat and mustard on the same land.

sections.heading: 3. The law of supply and market supply
sections.body_md:
**Law of supply:** other things constant, quantity supplied **rises** with price and **falls** with it; the curve slopes **upward**, because extra output usually costs more and a higher price makes it profitable.

**Market supply** is the **horizontal sum** of individual supplies: add quantities at each price.

sections.heading: 4. Exceptions to the law of supply
sections.body_md:
- **Labour:** beyond a high wage the supply curve **bends backward** as workers prefer leisure.
- **Rare goods:** quantity cannot be increased.
- **Agricultural goods:** output fixed until the next season.
- **Expectations:** a trader expecting a price rise may **withhold** stock now.

sections.heading: 6. Elasticity of supply

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Defining supply without a price and a period, or treating it as the same as stock.
- Calling a change caused by the own price a shift, or a change caused by costs an extension.
- Adding prices instead of quantities when deriving market supply.
- Dividing by the new values instead of the original ones in the percentage method.
- Judging elasticity of a straight supply line by its slope instead of where it meets the axes.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option or term.
- 2 marks: definition with an example, or formula and answer.
- 3 marks: working, answer and the degree, or three explained points.
- 5 marks: parts answered in order, with described diagrams and reasons.

questions.stem_md: In economics, the supply of a good means

options.text_md: the total quantity of the good lying in the warehouses of all sellers
the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a given period
the quantity that buyers wish to purchase at a given price
the quantity of the good produced since the firm began business

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price during a given period. Supply is always tied to a price and a period: it is the amount offered for sale. What sits in warehouses is stock; what buyers wish to purchase is demand.

questions.stem_md: A fisherman landing 500 kg of mackerel at an imagined Kochi harbour has no ice box and must sell the catch before evening. For him, supply at the ruling price is most likely

options.text_md: much smaller than his stock, because he can store fish for a better price
zero, because supply depends only on next week's price
greater than his stock, because supply includes future catches
almost equal to his stock, because the fish is perishable

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** almost equal to his stock, because the fish is perishable. A perishable good cannot be held back, so nearly the whole stock is offered for sale and supply is close to stock. Supply can never exceed the stock available in the period.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Saharanpur woodcraft dealer has 300 carved boxes in his godown but offers only 120 for sale at this month's price. How many boxes is he holding back in the hope of a better price?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 180. Stock is 300 and supply is 120, so 300 − 120 = 180 boxes are held back. A durable good can be stored, so supply may be well below stock.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Within a given short period, a seller's supply of a good can at most equal the stock of that good available to him.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Supply is drawn out of the existing stock in the short period, so it can equal the stock (as with perishables) but never exceed it.

questions.stem_md: Supply is the quantity offered for sale at a particular price during a particular ___ of time.
questions.solution_md: Supply always refers to a price and a period of time, which is why it is a flow concept.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between stock and supply, with one imagined example from an Indian market.
questions.solution_md: Define both and add one example where supply is less than stock.

answer.model_answer_md: **Stock** is the **total quantity** of a good a seller **has** at a point of time; **supply** is the part of it **offered for sale at a given price** in a period. A grain dealer in an imagined Agra mandi may hold 900 sacks but offer only 600 at today's price.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the gap between stock and supply is usually small for fresh coriander bunches but can be large for steel almirahs. Give one condition under which the almirah seller would release his whole stock.
questions.solution_md: Perishability links supply to stock; durability allows holding back; one release condition.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Coriander** is **perishable**: it wilts within a day, so the seller must offer nearly the **whole stock** at the ruling price; supply is close to stock.
2. **Almirahs** are **durable**: they can be stored without loss, so the seller may hold many back and supply **well below stock** when he expects prices to rise.
3. He would release the whole stock if the **price rose high enough** (or he expected prices to fall, or needed cash urgently).

marking_scheme.step: Perishable good: supply close to stock
Durable good: supply can be below stock
Condition for releasing the whole stock

questions.stem_md: The price of cotton yarn falls sharply for weavers in an imagined Bhiwandi powerloom cluster. Other things equal, the supply of grey cloth will

options.text_md: decrease: the supply curve shifts to the left
extend along the same supply curve
increase: the supply curve shifts to the right
stay the same, because only the price of cloth affects supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** increase: the supply curve shifts to the right. Cheaper inputs lower the cost of production, so more cloth is offered at every price: an increase in supply and a rightward shift. Extension needs a change in the cloth's own price.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Rajkot pump maker installs computer-controlled lathes that cut the time needed for each pump. The most likely effect on its supply curve is

options.text_md: a shift to the left, as machines are costly to install
a movement up the same curve
a shift to the right, as cost per pump falls
no change, because technology is not a determinant of supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a shift to the right, as cost per pump falls. Better technology lowers the cost of producing each unit, so the firm offers more at every price: the supply curve shifts right.

questions.stem_md: A state government places a new tax of ₹10 on every bottle of soft drink produced in an imagined Haridwar bottling plant. How does this affect the plant's supply?

options.text_md: Supply decreases: the curve shifts left because each bottle now costs more to sell
Supply increases: the curve shifts right as the plant earns tax refunds
Supply extends as the price buyers pay rises
Supply is unchanged because the tax is paid by buyers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Supply decreases: the curve shifts left because each bottle now costs more to sell. A tax per unit raises the cost of supplying each bottle, so less is offered at every price: a decrease in supply and a leftward shift.

questions.stem_md: Solar-panel makers in an imagined Gujarat industrial park receive a production subsidy of ₹2,000 for each panel. Which change in supply follows?

options.text_md: A contraction of supply along the same curve
A decrease in supply, shown by a leftward shift
An extension of supply caused by a rise in the panel price
An increase in supply, shown by a rightward shift

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** An increase in supply, shown by a rightward shift. A per-unit subsidy lowers the effective cost of each panel, so more panels are offered at every price: supply increases and the curve shifts right.

questions.stem_md: Farmers in an imagined Rajasthan district can sow either mustard or wheat in the rabi season. The price of mustard rises steeply while the wheat price is unchanged. Next season the supply of wheat from the district is likely to

options.text_md: increase, as farmers earn more from mustard
decrease, as land and effort shift to the more rewarding crop
extend, because the price of wheat has risen
stay unchanged, since the wheat price did not change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** decrease, as land and effort shift to the more rewarding crop. Wheat and mustard compete for the same land. A higher price of a related (competing) good draws resources away, so wheat supply decreases even though its own price is unchanged.

questions.stem_md: An imagined e-bike start-up in Bengaluru decides to aim for the largest market share rather than the largest profit. Compared with a profit-maximising rival with identical costs, at each price it will usually

options.text_md: offer a larger quantity for sale
offer a smaller quantity for sale
offer exactly the same quantity
stop supplying altogether

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** offer a larger quantity for sale. The goal of the firm is a determinant of supply. A firm aiming at sales or market share is willing to sell more at each price than one aiming only at maximum profit.

questions.stem_md: Twelve new bakeries open in an imagined Mysuru town over a year. The market supply of bread in the town will

options.text_md: decrease, because each bakery now sells less
increase, because more sellers offer bread at every price
extend only if the price of bread rises
not change, because market supply depends only on price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** increase, because more sellers offer bread at every price. Market supply is the sum of individual supplies, so more sellers raise the quantity offered at every price: an increase in market supply.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An improvement in the technology of a Ludhiana bicycle maker shifts its supply curve to the right.

**Reason (R):** Better technology works by raising the market price of bicycles.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion.
Assertion is true but Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: better technology lowers the cost of each bicycle, so more is offered at every price. R is false: technology acts through cost, not by raising the price of the good; a change in price would only move the firm along its curve.

questions.stem_md: Write the supply function for a good X in symbols and explain what any two of its variables stand for.
questions.solution_md: Function in symbols and two variables explained.

answer.model_answer_md: **Sx = f(Px, Pf, T, Tx, G, Pr, N)**. **Px** is the **own price** of X, the main variable on which quantity supplied depends; **Pf** is the **prices of factors** (inputs), whose rise raises cost and reduces supply.

questions.stem_md: Explain how a per-unit tax and a per-unit subsidy would each change the supply of LED bulbs from an imagined Noida factory.
questions.solution_md: Tax shifts left; subsidy shifts right, both through cost.

answer.model_answer_md: A **per-unit tax** adds to the **cost** of each bulb, so the factory offers **fewer bulbs at every price**: supply **decreases** (curve shifts left). A **subsidy** reduces the effective cost, so it offers **more at every price**: supply **increases** (curve shifts right).

questions.stem_md: A dairy cooperative in an imagined Anand village can turn its milk into either paneer or ghee. Explain how (i) a rise in the price of ghee, (ii) a fall in the price of fodder and (iii) a decision to win more customers will affect its supply of paneer.
questions.solution_md: Related good, input price and goal of the firm, each with direction.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Ghee is a **competing product**: a higher ghee price draws milk away from paneer, so paneer supply **decreases**.
(ii) Cheaper **fodder** lowers the **cost** of milk, so more paneer is offered at every price: supply **increases**.
(iii) Aiming to **win customers** (sales rather than profit) makes the cooperative offer **more** paneer at each price: supply **increases**.

questions.stem_md: State three causes that would decrease the supply of cement from an imagined plant in Satna, other than a change in the price of cement, and explain each briefly.
questions.solution_md: Three non-price causes, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **rise in input prices** such as coal or limestone raises **cost per bag**, so fewer bags are offered at each price.
2. A **new tax** on each bag of cement adds to cost and reduces supply.
3. **Outdated or failed machinery**, or a strike, reduces output at every price.
Each shifts the supply curve to the **left**.

questions.stem_md: Explain any five determinants of the supply of a good, using an imagined handloom unit in Varanasi as your example, and say in each case whether supply increases or decreases.
questions.solution_md: Five determinants with the direction of change.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Own price:** a higher price for Banarasi sarees makes larger output **profitable**, so quantity supplied **rises** (law of supply).
2. **Prices of inputs:** dearer **silk yarn** raises cost, so supply **decreases**.
3. **Technology:** **jacquard looms** cut cost per saree, so supply **increases**.
4. **Taxes and subsidies:** a **tax** on each saree reduces supply; a **subsidy** for weavers raises it.
5. **Prices of related goods:** if **dupattas** made on the same looms fetch more, looms shift to them and saree supply **decreases**.

marking_scheme.step: Related goods (or goal, number of firms)

questions.stem_md: The law of supply states that, other things remaining the same,

options.text_md: quantity supplied falls when the price of the good rises
supply always equals demand at every price
quantity supplied rises when the price of the good rises and falls when it falls
price rises whenever the quantity supplied rises

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** quantity supplied rises when the price of the good rises and falls when it falls. Price and quantity supplied move in the same direction, other things constant, so the supply curve slopes upward.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an extension of supply and an increase in supply.

answer.model_answer_md: An **extension** is a **movement up** the same supply curve caused by a **rise in the good's own price**. An **increase** is a **rightward shift** of the whole curve caused by a **non-price factor**, such as cheaper inputs, so more is offered at every price.

questions.stem_md: Using the imagined Surat weaver's data, describe two diagrams: one showing the price rising from ₹500 to ₹600, and one showing a fall in the cost of silk yarn. Name the change in each.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Distinguish between a contraction of supply and a decrease in supply, with described diagrams. [3]

questions.solution_md: Contraction versus decrease with diagrams; two applications.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A **contraction** is a **movement down** the same supply curve when the good's **own price falls**: less is offered at a lower price, the point sliding down S1. A **decrease** is a **leftward shift** of the whole curve from S1 to S2 when a **non-price factor** worsens, such as dearer inputs or a new tax: less is offered at **every** price. The first changes position on one curve; the second moves the curve itself.
(b) (i) A fall in the price of covers causes a **contraction**: the factory moves **down** its existing curve. (ii) Higher **wages** raise the **cost** of each cover, so less is offered at every price: a **decrease**, the curve shifting **left**.

questions.stem_md: Price elasticity of supply measures

options.text_md: the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in income
the change in a firm's cost when output changes
the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price
the total revenue a firm earns at a given price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's own price. Es compares the percentage change in quantity supplied with the percentage change in the good's own price.

questions.stem_md: By the percentage method, elasticity of supply equals

options.text_md: percentage change in price ÷ percentage change in quantity supplied
change in quantity supplied ÷ change in price
percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price
percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price. Es = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P): the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

questions.stem_md: This week a small Darjeeling tea garden (imagined) has exactly 80 kg of hand-rolled tea; a 10 per cent rise in price leaves the quantity it offers unchanged. Its elasticity of supply this week is

infinite: perfectly elastic supply, a horizontal curve
one: unitary elastic supply
greater than one: relatively elastic supply

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** zero: perfectly inelastic supply, a vertical curve. Quantity does not respond at all, so Es = 0 ÷ 10 = 0: perfectly inelastic, drawn as a vertical supply curve.

questions.stem_md: A supply curve that is a horizontal straight line shows that

options.text_md: quantity supplied stays fixed whatever the price (Es zero)

sellers will supply any quantity at one price and none below it (Es infinite)

questions.stem_md: Two straight-line supply curves both start from the origin, one steep and one flat. Their elasticities of supply are

options.text_md: greater than one for the flat line and less than one for the steep line
both equal to one at every point
less than one for the flat line and greater than one for the steep line
zero for the steep line and infinite for the flat line

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** both equal to one at every point. For any straight line from the origin, P ÷ Q equals the reciprocal of its slope, so Es = (ΔQ ÷ ΔP) × (P ÷ Q) = 1 whatever the slope.

zero at every point

questions.stem_md: A straight supply line for brass lamps from an imagined Moradabad unit, when extended, cuts the quantity (horizontal) axis to the right of the origin. Supply on this line is

perfectly elastic

questions.stem_md: An imagined Surat weaver raises her supply of silk sarees from 40 to 52 a week when the price rises from ₹500 to ₹600. Calculate her elasticity of supply by the percentage method.

questions.stem_md: Define elasticity of supply and write its formula by the percentage method.
questions.solution_md: Definition and formula.

answer.model_answer_md: **Elasticity of supply** is the degree of **responsiveness** of the **quantity supplied** of a good to a change in its **own price**. **Es = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price = (ΔQ ÷ Q) ÷ (ΔP ÷ P)**.

questions.stem_md: How does the geometric method tell us the elasticity of a straight-line supply curve from where it meets the axes?
questions.solution_md: Three intercept cases.

answer.model_answer_md: Extend the line to the axes. If it meets the **price axis**, **Es > 1**; if it passes through the **origin**, **Es = 1**; if it meets the **quantity axis**, **Es < 1**. A **horizontal** line is perfectly elastic and a **vertical** line perfectly inelastic.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Moradabad unit raises its monthly supply of brass lamps from 120 to 135 when the price goes up from ₹800 to ₹1,000. Calculate the elasticity of supply and state its degree, and suggest one reason for this degree.
questions.solution_md: Calculation, degree and a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Percentage change in quantity = 15 ÷ 120 × 100 = **12.5**; percentage change in price = 200 ÷ 800 × 100 = **25**; **Es = 12.5 ÷ 25 = 0.5**. Supply is **relatively inelastic**. Hand-beaten brass needs **skilled artisans** who cannot be hired quickly, so output responds slowly to price.

questions.stem_md: Three straight supply lines are drawn with price on the vertical axis. Line A, extended, meets the price axis; line B starts at the origin; line C, extended, meets the quantity axis. Identify the elasticity of supply on each and justify one of your answers.
questions.solution_md: Three identifications and one justification.

answer.model_answer_md: **Line A:** **Es > 1** (relatively elastic). **Line B:** **Es = 1** (unitary). **Line C:** **Es < 1** (relatively inelastic). **Justification for B:** on a line from the origin, Q is a fixed multiple of P, so any percentage change in price brings the **same percentage change** in quantity supplied.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Kanpur workshop's elasticity of supply of leather belts is 2. It supplies 300 belts a week at ₹150. Find the price at which it will supply 360 belts, showing your working.

answer.model_answer_md: Percentage rise in quantity = 60 ÷ 300 × 100 = **20**. Since Es = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price, the % change in price = 20 ÷ 2 = **10**. New price = ₹150 + 10 per cent of ₹150 = **₹165**.

questions.stem_md:
(a) An imagined Surat weaver supplies 40 silk sarees a week at ₹500 and 52 at ₹600. Calculate her elasticity of supply and state its degree. [2]
(b) An imagined Nashik onion trader has an elasticity of supply of 0.5 and supplies 1,000 kg a day at ₹20. Find his supply at ₹24 a kg, and explain why such a trader's supply might be inelastic. [3]
questions.solution_md: Two percentage-method calculations and a reason for inelastic supply.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Quantity rises 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = **30 per cent**; price rises 100 ÷ 500 × 100 = **20 per cent**; **Es = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5**, so supply is **relatively elastic**.
(b) Price rises 4 ÷ 20 × 100 = **20 per cent**, so quantity rises 0.5 × 20 = **10 per cent**: new supply = 1,000 + 100 = **1,100 kg**. Supply is inelastic because onions come from a crop already **harvested**; the trader can release only what he has in **storage**, and fresh output cannot be raised until the **next season**.

questions.stem_md: Explain the five degrees of elasticity of supply with described diagrams, and state how the geometric method identifies three of them from straight supply lines.
questions.solution_md: Five degrees with diagrams; three intercept cases.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Perfectly elastic (Es = ∞):** a **horizontal** line; any quantity at one price.
2. **Perfectly inelastic (Es = 0):** a **vertical** line; quantity fixed whatever the price.
3. **Unitary (Es = 1):** quantity changes in the **same proportion** as price.
4. **Relatively elastic (Es > 1):** quantity changes **more** than in proportion.
5. **Relatively inelastic (Es < 1):** quantity changes **less** than in proportion.
**Geometric method:** a straight line through the **origin** gives Es = 1; one meeting the **price axis** gives Es > 1; one meeting the **quantity axis** gives Es < 1.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Why can supply never be greater than stock in the short period, and why may it be much smaller? [2]
(b) A trader in an imagined Guntur chilli market expects chilli prices to rise sharply next month. Explain how this expectation can make his supply behave against the law of supply this month, and describe it on a diagram. [3]
questions.solution_md: Stock limit and holding back; expectations as an exception.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Supply is drawn from the **stock** available in the period, so it can at most **equal** it. It may be much **smaller** when the good is **durable** and sellers **hold back** part of the stock for a better price.
(b) Chillies can be **stored**, so the trader **withholds** stock now to sell at the higher expected price. Even if this month's price rises a little, he offers **less**, not more: quantity supplied moves **opposite** to the current price, an **exception** to the law. On a diagram with price on the y-axis, his offers this month fall back to the **left** as the price rises, instead of moving up an upward-sloping curve.

questions.stem_md:

(ii) Her neighbour Kavita bought a faster loom and now offers more sarees at every price. Name this change and say how it differs from Meera's change.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Quantity rises **30 per cent** (12 ÷ 40) and price **20 per cent** (100 ÷ 500), so **Es = 1.5**: relatively elastic.
(ii) Kavita shows an **increase in supply**: her whole curve **shifts right** because of **better technology**. Meera's change is an **extension**, a **movement along** her existing curve caused only by the **higher price**.

questions.stem_md:

(ii) Suggest what the dealer might do if he expected the price of boxes to fall next month, and why.
questions.solution_md: Perishable versus durable; expectations of a price fall.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Fish is **perishable**, so the fisherman must sell almost his **entire stock** today: supply equals stock. Boxes are **durable**, so the dealer can **store** them and offers only 120, holding back **180** for a better price.
(ii) Expecting a **fall** in price, he would **release more** of his stock **now**, since waiting would bring a lower price. His current supply would **rise** towards his stock.

(i) A straight supply line for cricket bats from an imagined Jalandhar factory, when extended, meets the price axis. State its elasticity of supply and justify your answer.
(ii) The supply curve of seats for a cricket match in an imagined stadium is vertical. Explain its elasticity and why it has this shape.
questions.solution_md: Geometric case and a fixed-quantity case.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Es is greater than one** (relatively elastic). By the **geometric method**, any straight supply line meeting the **price axis** has a quantity response **more than proportional** to the price change, since its price-to-quantity ratio exceeds the inverse of its slope.
(ii) **Es = 0** (perfectly inelastic). The stadium has a **fixed number of seats**, so however high the ticket price goes, no more seats can be offered for that match.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) Explain any four determinants of supply other than the good's own price, using an imagined Tiruppur garment exporter.
(ii) With described diagrams, distinguish between an increase in supply and an extension of supply, and say which of your four determinants could cause an increase.
questions.solution_md: Four non-price determinants; increase versus extension with diagrams.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Input prices:** a fall in the price of cotton yarn cuts cost and raises supply. **Technology:** automatic cutting machines lower cost per shirt and raise supply. **Taxes and subsidies:** an export subsidy raises supply; a new tax reduces it. **Related goods:** if knitted T-shirts made on the same lines fetch more, resources move to them and shirt supply falls.
(ii) An **extension** is a **movement up** one supply curve caused by a **higher own price**: from point A to point B on S1. An **increase** is a **rightward shift** from S1 to S2: **more is offered at every price** because a **non-price factor** has improved. Cheaper yarn, better technology or a subsidy could each cause an **increase**; a higher price of a related good would instead cause a decrease.

questions.stem_md:
Answer both parts. [4 + 4]

(i) An imagined Coimbatore maker cut its monthly supply of water pumps from 250 to 220 when the price fell from ₹4,000 to ₹3,600. Calculate its elasticity of supply, state the degree, and describe where its straight supply line would meet the axes.
(ii) Evaluate whether the market supply of pumps in the region would be more or less elastic than that of a single maker over a period of two years, giving reasons.
questions.solution_md: Percentage-method Es with geometric placement; reasoned evaluation over time.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) Quantity falls 30 ÷ 250 × 100 = **12 per cent**; price falls 400 ÷ 4,000 × 100 = **10 per cent**; **Es = 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2**, so supply is **relatively elastic**. By the geometric method, a straight line with Es above one, when extended, meets the **price axis** above the origin.
(ii) Over two years market supply would tend to be **more elastic**. Existing makers can **add machines and workers**, so output responds more fully to price. **New firms** can **enter** when prices are high and weak firms **leave** when prices fall, adding to the response. Against this, if a key input such as **specialised castings** were scarce, the response could stay **limited**. On balance the longer period and the entry of firms make market supply more responsive than one maker's supply in a single month.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined case about three Ludhiana knitting units and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined businesses and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Add the three units at ₹200: 20 + 15 + 10 = 45 packets.

**(b)** Price below cost.

**(c) (i)** Es = 1.333.

**OR (c) (ii)** Horizontal summation.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **45 packets**

**(b)** At ₹100 the price does **not cover its cost** of knitting a packet, so supplying would bring a **loss**; it starts supplying only at a higher price.

**(c) (i)** Quantity rises from 45 to 75, i.e. 30 ÷ 45 × 100 = **66.667 per cent**; price rises **50 per cent**; **Es = 66.667 ÷ 50 = 1.333**: **relatively elastic**.

**OR (c) (ii)** The market curve is the **horizontal sum** of the three curves: at each price, their **quantities are added**. It therefore lies to the **right** of every unit's curve and also slopes **upward**.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined diary of a Surat weaver and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice; the weaver and figures are imagined.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Quantity rises 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30 per cent; price rises 100 ÷ 500 × 100 = 20 per cent; Es = 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.

**(b)** Increase, rightward shift.

**(c) (i)** Decrease from fewer firms.

**OR (c) (ii)** Extension versus increase.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **1.5**

**(b)** An **increase in supply**: more sarees at the **same price**, so her supply curve **shifts right** because of cheaper yarn.

**(c) (i)** Fewer weavers means fewer quantities to add at each price, so **market supply decreases**: the market curve **shifts left**. It is caused by the **number of sellers**, not by the saree price.

**OR (c) (ii)** March shows an **extension**: a **movement up** the same curve caused by a **higher saree price**. June shows an **increase**: a **rightward shift** of the curve caused by **cheaper yarn**, with more offered at the same price.

questions.stem_md: Read the imagined report from a weekly haat in Odisha and answer the questions that follow. *(Written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** No change in quantity.

**(b)** Stock versus supply.

**(c) (i)** Ranking by how quickly quantity can respond.

**OR (c) (ii)** Quick access to stock and durability.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Zero (perfectly inelastic)**: the quantity offered did not change when the price rose.

**(b)** His **stock** is the whole stack of pots; his **supply** is only the number he **offers for sale** at the day's price, with the rest kept back.

**(c) (i)** **Fishermen (Es = 0)** cannot add to the morning's catch; the **potter** adds a little from his stack, so supply is **relatively inelastic**; the **clothes trader** can bring stock quickly, so supply is **relatively elastic**. Order: **fishermen, potter, clothes trader**.

**OR (c) (ii)** He can obtain **extra stock quickly** from a nearby warehouse and dhotis are **durable**, so a higher price calls out a **more than proportionate** rise in quantity: supply is **relatively elastic**.
